title: An-Nur, the Light
hook: the Light of the heavens and the earth, light upon light (24:35)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Hayy and al-Qayyum, the Living and the one who keeps all standing. Your line was everything rests on him. Did you feel the bed hold you last night? Day two hundred fifty-five.

Picture a house in Medina, fourteen hundred years ago, after dark. No electricity, no streetlights. In the wall there's a small hollow, a niche, and in it a clay lamp with a wick floating in olive oil. It's the only light in the room. Everyone's face turns toward it. You can see the edge of the flame, the glow on the wall, the little circle of the world it makes safe. Now imagine someone takes that ordinary, everyday lamp, the one every listener had in their own home, and uses it to describe God. That's what one of the most famous verses in the Qur'an does. Today: An-Nur.
screen: `A HOUSE AFTER DARK.` → `A LAMP IN A NICHE.` → `A PICTURE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Surah 24 is called an-Nur, the Light, and its thirty-fifth verse is called the Light Verse. In Pickthall's translation it opens: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." Then the picture. His light is like a niche, and in the niche a lamp. The lamp is in a glass, and the glass is like a shining star. The lamp is lit from the oil of a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, oil so pure it would almost glow on its own, even if no fire touched it. And then two words: "Light upon light." In Arabic, nurun 'ala nur. Look at the layers: a niche that gathers the light, a glass that makes it shine like a star, oil that nearly lights itself, a flame. Each one adds to the one before. Light upon light. The verse ends by saying God guides to his light whom he wills, and that he strikes these likenesses for people. Commentators have read the picture in many ways. Some say the lamp is the light of guidance in a believer's heart: the chest is the niche, the heart the glass, faith the flame. Some say it's the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, or the Qur'an. The great scholar al-Ghazali wrote a whole book on this one verse, the Niche of Lights. And the Prophet had a du'a asking God to put light in his heart, in his hearing, in his sight, on his right and his left, above and below him, and to make him light. He didn't ask for a lamp. He asked to be one.
screen: `THE LIGHT OF THE HEAVENS AND EARTH.` · `NICHE, GLASS, OIL, FLAME.` · `THE HEART, THE PROPHET, THE BOOK.` · `MAKE ME LIGHT.` · then, large: `LIGHT UPON LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit near a lamp or a window. Move there now if you can. Let your eyes rest on the light, softly, not staring. Notice the layers: the source, the glass or the shade, the glow it throws on the wall, the light landing on your hands. Light upon light. Then close your eyes and notice that the light is still there, faintly, through your eyelids. If you pray, you can ask God, an-Nur, for light in your heart. The bell holds the time.
An-Nur. The Light: the Light of the heavens and the earth, pictured as a lamp in a niche, light upon light. Today's word.
Your line: light upon light. Today, every time you switch on a light, let it remind you of the lamp in the niche, just for a second. Day two hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: The Light Verse is one of the most often calligraphed verses in mosques and homes, and many Muslims say the Prophet's du'a for light, often on the way to the dawn prayer.

fork.setup: the verse describes the olive tree the oil comes from. where does it grow?
options: in the east, where the sun rises.
in the west, where it sets.
neither of the east nor of the west.
fork.reveal: neither of the east nor of the west. commentators say it catches the sun all day, and many read it as beyond any one place.

original.note: Arabic: light upon light (24:35). an-Nur, the Light, names the whole surah.

trapdoor: what you thought: God is light, a nice image.
what it means: a lamp in a niche, in a glass like a star, lit from oil that almost glows alone: light upon light.
what a scholar hears: the Light Verse has a whole literature of its own, above all al-Ghazali's Mishkat al-Anwar, which reads each layer of the lamp.
